studies.title: Analysis of the 2028/2029 RPM Base Residual Auction - Part A
studies.author_org: Monitoring Analytics (Independent Market Monitor for PJM)
studies.claim: Data-center load (existing plus forecast) is the primary reason for PJM's tight supply, capacity shortfalls and high capacity prices; there would have been no shortfall in the last three auctions but for forecast data-center load.
studies.notes: Table 1 of this report is the single best source for the per-auction data-center cost series. A circulating '2027/28 ~ $6.3bn' figure does not match the IMM: 2027/28 is $6.50bn (all data-center load) or $6.24bn (forecast growth only); $6.27bn is the 2028/29 figure. Auction revenue is not identical to cost to load (self-supply and bilateral hedges).

studies.title: Analysis of the 2025/2026 RPM Base Residual Auction - Part G (Revised)
studies.author_org: Monitoring Analytics (Independent Market Monitor for PJM)
studies.claim: Inclusion of existing and forecast data-center load in the peak-load forecast raised 2025/26 capacity auction revenues by about $9.3bn.
studies.notes: Numbers verified from Table 1 of the IMM 2028/29 Part A, which cites this report; PDF also saved in data/raw/markets.

studies.title: Analysis of the 2027/2028 RPM Base Residual Auction - Part A
studies.author_org: Monitoring Analytics (Independent Market Monitor for PJM)
studies.claim: Data-center load raised 2027/28 auction revenues by about $6.5bn; cumulative impact of the last three auctions above $23bn.
studies.notes: Also cited by Maryland OPC's FERC complaint ('more than $6.5 billion' and 'over $23 billion over the last three auctions').

studies.title: 2025 State of the Market Report for PJM, Section 5: Capacity Market
studies.author_org: Monitoring Analytics (Independent Market Monitor for PJM)
studies.claim: RPM capacity revenue jumped from $2.6bn (2024/25 delivery year) to $14.9bn (2025/26) and $16.1-16.4bn for 2026/27-2027/28; annual capacity charges to load rose from $2.5bn to $14.8bn.
studies.notes: Descriptive (sizes the capacity bill), not an attribution study by itself.

studies.title: Data Center Growth Could Increase Electricity Bills 8% Nationally and as Much as 25% in Some Regional Markets
studies.author_org: Carnegie Mellon University & NC State University (Open Energy Outlook Initiative): Blackhurst, Wade, DeCarolis, de Queiroz, Johnson, Jaramillo
studies.claim: Data-center and crypto-mining growth through 2030 could raise average US electricity generation costs 8%, with central and northern Virginia above 25%; keeps >25 GW of coal running and raises power-sector CO2 30%.
studies.notes: The 8% is a generation-cost increase that press often reports as 'bills'. A 2026 peer-reviewed version (Environmental Research Letters, NC State release May 2026) reportedly gives a 6-29% national range and up to 57% locally and 'up to 28%' CO2; that release returned HTTP 403 and is UNVERIFIED.

studies.title: Connection Costs: Loophole Costs Customers Over $4 Billion to Connect Data Centers to Power Grid (policy brief + appendix)
studies.author_org: Union of Concerned Scientists (Mike Jacobs)
studies.claim: Utilities in seven PJM states approved $4.36bn of transmission projects in 2024 solely to connect individual data centers; over 95% of the projects pass all costs to all customers through formula transmission rates.
studies.region: PJM: IL, MD, NJ, OH, PA, VA, WV
studies.notes: Counts only direct connection (supplemental) projects, not regional backbone upgrades. These costs are spread by FERC formula rates, which do not track which customer caused them.

studies.title: Extracting Profits from the Public: How Utility Ratepayers Are Paying for Big Tech's Power
studies.author_org: Harvard Law School Electricity Law Initiative (Eliza Martin, Ari Peskoe)
studies.claim: Utility rate structures, confidential special contracts and the federal/state transmission cost-allocation gap let utilities shift data-center costs to captive ratepayers while utilities profit from new rate base.
studies.notes: Qualitative: it does not estimate a dollar amount of cost shift. Recommends special contracts that cover cost of service, tariffs for all new data centers, disclosure of forecasts, and flexible-operation requirements.

studies.title: Factors Impacting Retail Electricity Prices in the United States (and 2025/2026 data updates)
studies.author_org: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory & The Brattle Group (Wiser, Barbose, Cappers et al.; Hledik et al.)
studies.claim: 2019-2024: states with the highest load growth generally saw real retail prices fall (fixed costs spread over more sales); distribution/transmission spending, storms/wildfires, RPS costs and gas prices drove increases. PJM is the exception: accelerated load growth plus supply and delivery constraints raised capacity prices.
studies.notes: Authors warn past relationship may not persist where supply/delivery is constrained. Primary pages: https://emp.lbl.gov/retail-electricity-price-trends-and-drivers (LBL PDFs returned HTTP 403 to scripts; read the January 2026 deck from the Montana Legislature mirror). A July 2026 update with a load-growth deep dive exists but was not read (403).

studies.title: Tailored for Scale: Amazon Data Center Case Studies (Ratepayer Study)
studies.author_org: Energy and Environmental Economics (E3), funded by Amazon
studies.claim: The Amazon data centers studied pay utility bills that meet or exceed their incremental cost to serve, producing surplus revenue that can put downward pressure on other customers' rates.
studies.notes: Funded and reviewed by Amazon. Does not model system-wide costs (regional transmission, capacity-market price effects) triggered by aggregate data-center growth, which is the IMM's main channel.

studies.title: Understanding the Drivers of Rising Electricity Rates and the Role of Data Centers
studies.author_org: Energy and Environmental Economics (E3), funded by the Data Center Coalition
studies.claim: No quantitative evidence to date that data centers have been subsidized by other customers; states with the most load growth (TX, VA) had the smallest rate increases; in PJM, load growth (mainly data centers) explains about half of the 2024/25 to 2025/26 capacity price jump.
studies.notes: Sponsor (DCC) reviewed the paper before publication. Note the tension with the IMM: E3 attributes ~50% of the 2025/26 increase to load growth and ~50% to market-design changes and retirements; the IMM's counterfactual attributes $9.3bn of $14.7bn (~63%) to data-center load.

studies.title: Large Load Tariff Whitepaper (benchmarking representative large-load tariffs)
studies.author_org: Energy and Environmental Economics (E3)
studies.claim: Annual bills for an identical hypothetical data-center load differ materially across utility large-load tariffs; minimum-demand/contract-capacity provisions shift ramp-up risk onto the data center, protecting other customers.
studies.notes: Useful for the 'who pays' panel; detailed per-tariff numbers are in figures not extracted here.

studies.title: Data Centers in Virginia (JLARC Report 598; E3 grid and rate modeling)
studies.author_org: Virginia Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, with E3
studies.claim: Current rates allocate costs appropriately (no historic cost shift), but unconstrained data-center growth will raise generation and transmission costs that are hard to assign, putting upward pressure on residential bills.
studies.notes: Press summaries cite 'nearly $40/month' or '$444/yr by 2040'; those figures were not found in the presentation text read here (UNVERIFIED). Full report: https://jlarc.virginia.gov/pdfs/reports/Rpt598.pdf

studies.title: Large load tariffs: a looming challenge for utilities (and follow-up on clean transition tariffs)
studies.author_org: Wood Mackenzie (Ben Hertz-Shargel)
studies.claim: Large-load tariffs (minimum contract terms, exit fees, collateral) are utilities' attempt to contain cost and risk but fall short for long-lived generation and transmission; transmission costs are hardest to confine to the large customer.
studies.notes: Full report not accessed; claim from Wood Mackenzie opinion page snippet, Utility Dive and Resources Radio summaries. No quantitative result recorded.

studies.title: AI Data Centers Are Sending Power Bills Soaring
studies.author_org: Bloomberg News (graphics/analysis)
studies.claim: Wholesale electricity prices at grid nodes near data-center clusters rose up to 267% over five years; many of the biggest jumps (e.g., Baltimore) are near data-center hot spots.
studies.notes: Paywalled; numbers from secondary coverage (Tom's Hardware, Sherwood, PolitiFact). Correlation, not causation; wholesale energy is roughly 30-50% of a retail bill and 2020 was a pandemic low-price baseline.

studies.title: Fact-check: Elizabeth Warren on data centers and rising electricity costs
studies.author_org: PolitiFact
studies.claim: Claim that residential bills rose 267% misrepresents Bloomberg's wholesale-price data, though data centers are a real driver of higher costs in some areas.
studies.notes: Read via search snippet only.

studies.title: Complaint of the Maryland Office of People's Counsel against PJM's hybrid transmission cost allocation (with Nelson & Eiden affidavit)
studies.author_org: Maryland Office of People's Counsel
studies.claim: PJM's hybrid cost allocation spreads data-center-driven regional transmission (RTEP 2022 W3, 2024 W1, 2025 W1; >$22bn baseline) across the footprint, assigning Maryland customers costs unrelated to Maryland load growth.
studies.region: PJM; Maryland (BGE, Pepco, Delmarva, Potomac Edison)
studies.notes: Covered by Bloomberg (2026-05-07) as 'AI push to add $1.6 billion to Maryland power bills'. Transmission costs begin 2029, peak 2033.

studies.title: PJM Board Annual Meeting: Maryland People's Counsel presentation on behalf of Consumer Advocates of PJM States (CAPS)
studies.author_org: Maryland Office of People's Counsel / CAPS
studies.claim: PJM wholesale costs are 55-70% of residential bills; PJM's 2026 forecast shows organic (non-data-center) load flat-to-negative for ten years, so data centers are the core cost driver and should be planned and charged separately.

studies.title: PJM Board to Decide on Higher Bills for 67 Million Americans Due to Data Centers
studies.author_org: Natural Resources Defense Council (with Citizens Utility Board briefing)
studies.claim: If data-center load keeps outrunning supply, PJM customers face about $163bn of capacity costs in 2028-2032 (through 2033) and recurring shortfalls; requiring data centers to bring their own capacity would cut costs by roughly $100bn.
studies.notes: $163bn read on the NRDC release; the $27-30bn/yr, $70/month and $100bn figures come from CUB/E&E secondary summaries (UNVERIFIED).

studies.title: Rapid Data Center Growth Risks Utility Bill & Emissions Increases in the Mid-Atlantic
studies.author_org: Sierra Club
studies.claim: Rapid data-center growth could raise average PJM residential bills about 10%, more in Virginia, and increase emissions.
studies.notes: Page redirected (HTTP 302) for scripts; figures from search snippet only. Sierra Club's 2027 legislative menu reports ~147 data-center guardrail bills in 34 states in 2026, ~25 passed (UNVERIFIED): https://www.sierraclub.org/sites/default/files/2026-08/2027-state-legislative-menu-for-data-center-guardrails.pdf

studies.title: Retail rate trends in the US
studies.author_org: Charles River Associates for Edison Electric Institute
studies.claim: Data centers did not trigger retail rate increases, with one exception (PJM capacity prices, partly due to data centers); recent increases are concentrated in the Northeast (wholesale prices) and California (wildfires).
studies.notes: Commissioned by the utility trade association.

studies.title: America's Electric Companies Are Protecting Customers and Powering Innovation (statement on White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge expansion)
studies.author_org: Edison Electric Institute
studies.claim: Connecting data centers responsibly spreads costs over more customers; cites Georgia PSC approving ~ $50/yr lower rates and an Alliant Iowa five-year residential rate freeze tied to data-center growth.
studies.notes: Advocacy by utilities, which earn returns on new rate base built for data centers.

studies.title: Have data centers raised your electric bill?
studies.author_org: EPRI (Energy Systems and Climate Analysis)
studies.claim: Causal evidence suggests data centers modestly lowered average US retail rates in 2015-2024 by spreading fixed costs over more demand.
studies.notes: URL returned 'page not found' to scripts; numbers from search snippets (incl. an LBNL literature review citing it). Backward-looking: does not cover the 2025+ PJM capacity shock.

studies.title: The Effects of Load Growth on Electricity Prices in the United States: A Literature Review
studies.author_org: Columbia University SIPA Center on Global Energy Policy (supported by Google.org)
studies.claim: Residential prices rose more than twice inflation in 2025, breaking the 2019-2024 pattern; increases come from layered regional pressures (grid hardening, disasters, fuel, mandates) not demand alone; 'beneficiary-pays' tariffs are emerging to stop cost shifts.
studies.notes: Funded by Google.org (a data-center operator's philanthropy).

studies.title: How the AI Data Center Boom Costs [Americans]: investigation of seven data-center operators
studies.author_org: Offices of Sens. Warren, Van Hollen and Blumenthal
studies.claim: Operators' 'fair share' pledges cover infrastructure built exclusively for their sites but not broader system upgrades; companies opposed 'but-for' cost allocation, seek NDAs and tax breaks, and play states against each other.
studies.notes: Partisan (Democratic senators') staff report; qualitative.

studies.title: Working paper on county-level retail rates after data-center entry
studies.author_org: Georgia Tech (working paper)
studies.claim: Small average increase in retail electricity rates in a subset of US counties after initial data-center entry.
studies.notes: Known only through E3's 2026 literature review; original paper not located.

studies.title: State load growth vs retail rate changes
studies.author_org: Bates White Economic Consulting
studies.claim: States with the largest load increases (Texas, Virginia) had the smallest rate increases; California and New York had the largest increases with falling load.
studies.notes: Known only through E3's 2026 literature review.
